metadata.content: Diabetes is a long-lasting condition that affects how the body turns food into energy. Food is broken down into sugar in the blood. In response, the body releases insulin, which moves that sugar into cells to be used for energy. In diabetes, the body either makes too little insulin or cannot use it well, so too much sugar stays in the blood. Over time, high blood sugar can lead to problems such as heart disease, vision loss and kidney disease. There is currently no cure for diabetes, but weight loss, healthy eating and regular physical activity can help.
metadata.title: Diabetes Basics (CDC)
metadata.heading: What diabetes is

metadata.content:
- **Type 1:** Thought to be caused by an autoimmune reaction in which the body stops making insulin. People with type 1 need insulin every day. It is usually diagnosed in children and young adults but can happen at any age. There is no known way to prevent it.
- **Type 2:** The body does not use insulin well and cannot keep blood sugar at a normal level. It develops over many years and is usually diagnosed in adults, although it is increasingly seen in children, teenagers and young adults. It can be prevented or delayed with lifestyle changes.
- **Gestational:** Develops during pregnancy in women who did not have diabetes before. It usually goes away after the baby is born, but it raises the mother's chance of type 2 diabetes later. The baby also has a higher chance of obesity and type 2 diabetes later in life.
metadata.title: Diabetes Basics (CDC)
metadata.heading: Types of diabetes

metadata.content: Early type 1 diabetes may cause no symptoms, and symptoms may then appear suddenly and strongly over weeks or months. Type 2 diabetes may also cause no noticeable symptoms for a long time, which is why blood sugar testing is advised for people at risk.
metadata.title: Diabetes Basics (CDC)
metadata.heading: Symptoms and awareness

metadata.content:
- Type 2 makes up about 90% to 95% of diagnosed cases and type 1 about 5% to 10%.
- Diabetes is a leading cause of kidney failure, lower-limb amputation and adult blindness.
This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page.
It does not diagnose any condition.
metadata.title: Diabetes Basics (CDC)
metadata.heading: Additional points from the page (United States data)

metadata.content: About half of people with diabetes have nerve damage, most often in the feet and legs. Nerve damage can reduce feeling, so a person may not notice a cut, blister or sore. Foot ulcers that are not treated can become infected and heal poorly, and serious infections may lead to amputation. Keeping blood sugar within the target range is one of the most important ways to prevent or slow nerve damage.
metadata.title: Your Feet and Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Why foot care matters

metadata.content:
- Check both feet every day for cuts, redness, swelling, sores, blisters, corns, calluses, and changes to skin or nails. A mirror or another person can help if it is hard to see.
- Wash feet daily in warm water, dry them well, and moisturise the tops and bottoms, but not between the toes.
- Wear shoes, socks or slippers at all times, even indoors, and check inside shoes for objects before putting them on.
- Choose well-fitting shoes, ideally bought when feet are largest (end of the day), and break new shoes in gradually.
- Trim toenails straight across and smooth sharp edges with a file. A foot specialist (podiatrist) can help if nails are hard to reach.
- Do not remove corns or calluses yourself, and avoid over-the-counter removal products.
- Help blood flow by raising feet when sitting and wiggling the toes several times a day.
- Ask a doctor which activities are suitable.
- Have feet checked at every primary care visit, and see a foot specialist once a year for a full exam, or more often if there is nerve damage.
metadata.title: Your Feet and Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Everyday foot care steps listed on the page

metadata.content:
- Leg pain or cramping in the buttocks, thighs or calves during activity
- Tingling, burning or pain in the feet
- Less ability to feel touch, heat or cold
- Changes in the shape of the foot over time
- Hair loss on the toes, feet or lower legs
- Dry, cracked skin
- Changes in foot colour or temperature
- Thick, yellow toenails
- Fungal infections such as athlete's foot
- A blister, sore, ulcer, infected corn or ingrown toenail
The page advises contacting a doctor or foot specialist right away if any warning sign appears, rather than waiting for the next appointment.
This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page.
It does not diagnose any condition.
metadata.title: Your Feet and Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Warning signs to tell a doctor about

metadata.content: Keeping blood sugar in a target range as much as possible helps prevent or delay serious health problems. The page lists general habits that support this: a healthy diet, a healthy weight, regular physical activity, eating at regular times without skipping meals, and tracking blood sugar to learn what makes it rise or fall.
metadata.title: Manage Blood Sugar (CDC)
metadata.heading: Why it matters

metadata.content:
- Choose lower-calorie foods, and limit saturated fat, sugar and salt.
- Drink water instead of juice or soda, and choose fruit for something sweet.
- Control portions, for example with the plate method.
- Carbohydrate counting is described as an important tool, and the page suggests talking with a healthcare team about carbohydrate goals.
- Alcohol: if drinking, no more than 2 drinks a day for men and 1 drink a day for women.
metadata.title: Manage Blood Sugar (CDC)
metadata.heading: General eating and drinking points on the page

metadata.content:
- Before a meal: 80 to 130 mg/dL
- Two hours after the start of a meal: below 180 mg/dL
- Low blood sugar: below 70 mg/dL
Targets can differ depending on age, other health conditions and other factors.
The page says to ask the healthcare team which targets are best for the individual.
metadata.title: Manage Blood Sugar (CDC)
metadata.heading: Target ranges mentioned (adults, US guidance)

metadata.content:
- A blood sugar meter (glucometer) or a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) can be used. A CGM uses a sensor under the skin to measure blood sugar every few minutes. People who use one may still need to check with a meter to confirm accuracy.
- Common times to check: on waking before eating or drinking, before meals, two hours after meals, and at bedtime.
- A doctor may advise more frequent checks for people with type 1 diabetes, people with type 2 diabetes who use insulin, or people who often have low blood sugar.
metadata.title: Manage Blood Sugar (CDC)
metadata.heading: Checking blood sugar

metadata.content: Blood sugar that is too high is called hyperglycemia. The page says it can be caused by being sick, being stressed, eating more than usual, or not taking enough insulin.
metadata.title: Manage Blood Sugar (CDC)
metadata.heading: High blood sugar (hyperglycemia)

metadata.content: If a person with diabetes is sick and their blood sugar is 240 mg/dL or above, the page suggests using an over-the-counter ketone test kit. High ketones can be an early sign of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which the page calls a medical emergency needing immediate treatment. A person should contact their doctor if ketones are high. This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page. It is not personal medical advice, and a person's own targets and schedule should come from their healthcare professional.
metadata.title: Manage Blood Sugar (CDC)
metadata.heading: Ketones and when to contact a doctor

metadata.content: The A1C test, also called the hemoglobin A1C or HbA1c test, is a simple blood test. It shows a person's average blood sugar over roughly the past 3 months. This is different from a home blood sugar check, which shows the level at one moment. The 3-month window exists because red blood cells renew about every 3 months. The test measures the percentage of red blood cells that have sugar attached to hemoglobin.
metadata.title: A1C Test for Diabetes and Prediabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: What it measures

metadata.content:
- To help diagnose prediabetes and diabetes.
- To monitor how well diabetes is being managed over time.
- It does not replace checking blood sugar at home.
- No fasting is needed for this test.
- Testing is recommended for people over 45, and for younger people who are overweight or have another risk factor for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes.
metadata.title: A1C Test for Diabetes and Prediabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: How it is used

metadata.content:
- Normal: below 5.7%
- Prediabetes: 5.7% to 6.4%
- Diabetes: 6.5% or above
metadata.title: A1C Test for Diabetes and Prediabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: A1C ranges given on the page (US guidance)

metadata.content:
- Normal result: the doctor sets a re-testing schedule based on age and risk factors.
- Prediabetes: repeated about every 1 to 2 years.
- Diabetes: most people are tested at least twice a year, sometimes more often depending on their plan or other health conditions.
metadata.title: A1C Test for Diabetes and Prediabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: How often it is repeated (as described on the page)

metadata.content: The A1C average may not show short spikes or dips in blood sugar. Some conditions can make the result read falsely high or low, including severe anemia, kidney failure, liver disease, some blood disorders (such as sickle cell disease or thalassemia), some medicines, blood loss or transfusion, and early or late pregnancy. The page advises telling the doctor if any of these apply. A single result is not a diagnosis, and individual targets are set by a healthcare professional. This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page.
metadata.title: A1C Test for Diabetes and Prediabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Things that can affect the result

metadata.content: Blood sugar below 70 mg/dL is considered low (hypoglycemia). The page says it can be dangerous if left untreated and is especially common in people with type 1 diabetes. Blood sugar below 54 mg/dL is described as severe low blood sugar.
metadata.title: Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia) (CDC)
metadata.heading: What it is

metadata.content:
- **Common:** fast heartbeat, shaking, sweating, nervousness or anxiety, irritability or confusion, dizziness and hunger.
- **Severe:** weakness, trouble walking or seeing clearly, strange behaviour or confusion, and seizures. Blood sugar this low can cause fainting. A person with severe low blood sugar will need someone else to help them.
- **Hypoglycemia unawareness:** some people have no warning symptoms. This is more likely if someone has had diabetes for more than 5 to 10 years, often has lows, or takes certain medicines such as beta blockers.
metadata.title: Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia) (CDC)
metadata.heading: Symptoms

metadata.content:
- Too much insulin, or insulin taken at the wrong time
- Not eating enough carbohydrate for the insulin dose
- Physical activity, including how much and when
- Drinking alcohol
- The fat, protein and fibre content of meals
- Hot and humid weather, or high altitude
- Unexpected changes in daily routine
- Puberty and menstruation
metadata.title: Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia) (CDC)
metadata.heading: Things that can contribute

metadata.content:
- Eat regular meals and do not skip them. This can help avoid lows at night.
- People at risk of lows overnight may be advised to have a snack before bed, and to eat when drinking alcohol.
- A continuous glucose monitor (CGM) can alert a person while they sleep.
- People with hypoglycemia unawareness may need to check blood sugar more often, especially before driving or physical activity.
metadata.title: Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia) (CDC)
metadata.heading: Ideas the page gives for reducing the chance of lows

metadata.content: The page does not give emergency instructions of its own. It mentions confusion, seizures and fainting as severe signs, and refers readers to a separate CDC page on treating low blood sugar. Anyone with severe symptoms, or who is unable to look after themselves, needs urgent medical help. Questions about medicines, insulin or what to do for lows should go to a healthcare professional. This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page.
metadata.title: Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia) (CDC)
metadata.heading: Notes

metadata.content: Diabetes is a long-term (chronic) condition. It happens when the pancreas does not make enough insulin, or when the body cannot use the insulin it makes effectively. Insulin is a hormone that helps regulate blood glucose (blood sugar). When blood glucose stays high for a long time (hyperglycaemia), it can gradually damage the body, especially the nerves and blood vessels.
metadata.title: Diabetes (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: What diabetes is

metadata.content:
- **Type 1 diabetes:** The body produces very little or no insulin, so daily insulin is needed. WHO says the cause and a way to prevent it are not known.
- **Type 2 diabetes:** The body cannot use insulin properly. It makes up more than 95% of all diabetes cases and is often preventable.
- **Gestational diabetes:** Blood glucose is higher than normal but below the level used to diagnose diabetes, and it appears during pregnancy. It is usually found through screening during prenatal care rather than through symptoms.
- **Impaired glucose tolerance and impaired fasting glycaemia:** These are in-between states. People with them have a high chance of developing type 2 diabetes, but it is not certain that they will.
metadata.title: Diabetes (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: Types of diabetes

metadata.content:
- Feeling very thirsty
- Passing urine more often than usual
- Blurred vision
- Feeling tired
- Losing weight without trying
Symptoms of type 2 diabetes can be mild and may take years to be noticed.
metadata.title: Diabetes (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: Common symptoms

metadata.content: The page mentions being overweight, not getting enough physical activity, and genetics.
metadata.title: Diabetes (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: Risk factors for type 2 diabetes

metadata.content:
- About 830 million people were living with diabetes in 2022, compared with 200 million in 1990.
- In 2022, 59% of adults aged 30 and over with diabetes were not taking medicine for it.
- Diabetes directly caused about 1.6 million deaths in 2021.
This is general educational information summarised from the WHO page.
It does not diagnose any condition.
A qualified healthcare professional can interpret symptoms and test results for an individual.
metadata.title: Diabetes (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: Scale of the problem (WHO figures)

metadata.content: The WHO date shown on the page is 26 January 2026. The page does not say whether it is the first publication date or the last update.
metadata.title: Healthy diet (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: Healthy diet for adults (WHO)

metadata.content:
- **Fruits and vegetables:** at least 400 grams a day.
- **Free sugars:** less than 10% of total daily energy. For a person of healthy weight eating about 2000 calories a day, that is about 50 grams (roughly 12 level teaspoons). Going down to 5% or less may bring extra benefits.
- **Fat:** total fat of 30% or less of daily energy; saturated fat under 10%; trans fat under 1%. Fat should still provide at least 15% of daily energy.
- **Salt:** less than 5 grams of salt a day (equal to 2 grams of sodium).
- **Potassium:** at least 3510 mg a day, which can help offset the effect of sodium on blood pressure.
- **Fibre and whole grains:** at least 25 grams of naturally occurring fibre a day. Carbohydrates should come mainly from whole grains, vegetables, fruits and pulses, and make up roughly 45% to 75% of daily energy.
metadata.title: Healthy diet (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: What WHO recommends for adults

metadata.content: Healthy diets help protect against malnutrition in all its forms and against noncommunicable diseases including diabetes, heart disease, stroke and cancer. Less sodium supports lower blood pressure. This is a general population recommendation and not an individual diet plan for a person with diabetes. A registered dietitian or doctor can advise on personal needs. This is general educational information summarised from the WHO page.
metadata.title: Healthy diet (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: Benefits WHO describes

metadata.content: Diabetic ketoacidosis is a serious, potentially life-threatening complication of diabetes. It is most common in people with type 1 diabetes, though people with type 2 diabetes can develop it too. It happens when there is too little insulin for sugar to enter the cells for energy. The liver then breaks down fat for fuel, which makes acids called ketones, and these can build up to dangerous levels. Sometimes DKA is the first sign of diabetes in someone who has not yet been diagnosed.
metadata.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (CDC)
metadata.heading: What DKA is

metadata.content:
- **Early signs, which usually develop slowly:** intense thirst and passing urine very often.
- **More serious signs, which can appear quickly:** fast, deep breathing; dry skin and mouth; a flushed face; fruity-smelling breath; headache; muscle stiffness or aches; extreme tiredness; nausea and vomiting; stomach pain.
metadata.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (CDC)
metadata.heading: Warning signs

metadata.content:
- Illness, which can make eating and drinking difficult and blood sugar harder to manage
- Missed insulin doses, a blocked insulin pump, or an incorrect insulin dose
- Less often: heart attack, stroke, physical injury, alcohol or drug use, and certain medicines
metadata.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (CDC)
metadata.heading: Common causes

metadata.content:
The page says to go to the emergency room or call emergency services right away (the page is written for the United States, where the number is 911) if a person has any of the following:
- Blood sugar that stays at 300 mg/dL or above
- Fruity-smelling breath
- Vomiting and being unable to keep food or drinks down
- Trouble breathing
- Several signs and symptoms of DKA together
The page also says that elevated ketones are a sign of DKA, which is a medical emergency needing immediate treatment.
metadata.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (CDC)
metadata.heading: When the page says to get emergency care

metadata.content: For a person with diabetes who is sick, or whose blood sugar is 250 mg/dL or above, the page advises checking blood sugar every 4 to 6 hours and checking urine for ketones. This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page. It is not a substitute for urgent medical care. Anyone with severe symptoms should seek emergency help immediately.
metadata.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (CDC)
metadata.heading: Checking when unwell

metadata.content:
- Passing urine more often
- Feeling more thirsty and hungry than usual
- Losing weight without trying
- Feeling tired
- Irritability or mood changes
- Blurred vision
- Urinary tract infections or yeast infections that keep coming back
metadata.title: Symptoms of Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Symptoms that can occur in both type 1 and type 2

metadata.content:
- Nausea
- Vomiting
- Stomach pain
- Diabetic ketoacidosis (a serious complication)
- In children, unexplained bed-wetting or more accidents than usual
metadata.title: Symptoms of Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Additional symptoms mentioned for type 1

metadata.content:
- Cuts, sores or wounds that heal very slowly
- Dark patches of skin around the neck, armpits or groin
- Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
metadata.title: Symptoms of Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Additional symptoms mentioned for type 2

metadata.content:
- Early type 1 diabetes may have no symptoms.
- Type 2 diabetes symptoms can take several years to develop, and some people never notice any.
- Gestational diabetes usually has no symptoms.
metadata.title: Symptoms of Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Diabetes can exist without symptoms

metadata.content: The page says a doctor should test for gestational diabetes between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. If lifestyle changes do not keep blood sugar under control, a doctor may prescribe medicine. These symptoms can have many causes, and having one does not mean a person has diabetes. A healthcare professional can arrange the right tests. This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page.
metadata.title: Symptoms of Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Gestational diabetes testing

metadata.content: These values come from the CDC page and are written for the United States. They are used by doctors to interpret test results. Guidelines in other countries can differ, so a person should ask their own doctor how results apply to them.
metadata.title: Diabetes Testing (CDC)
metadata.heading: Diabetes testing (CDC)

metadata.content:
- **A1C test:** Shows average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months. Normal is below 5.7%, prediabetes is 5.7% to 6.4%, and diabetes is 6.5% or above.
- **Fasting blood sugar test:** Done after an overnight fast. Normal is 99 mg/dL or below, prediabetes is 100 to 125 mg/dL, and diabetes is 126 mg/dL or above.
- **Glucose tolerance test:** Blood sugar is measured while fasting and again after drinking a sugary liquid, usually at 1, 2 and sometimes 3 hours. At 2 hours, normal is 140 mg/dL or below, prediabetes is 140 to 199 mg/dL, and diabetes is 200 mg/dL or above.
- **Random blood sugar test:** Done at any time without fasting. A result of 200 mg/dL or above points to diabetes.
- **Autoantibody test:** A blood test that looks for substances linked to type 1 diabetes.
- **Urine ketone test:** Mentioned in relation to type 1 diabetes.
- **Gestational diabetes tests:** A glucose screening test (a sugary drink followed by a blood sample 1 hour later, where 140 mg/dL or lower is normal), and a glucose tolerance test if the screening result is higher.
metadata.title: Diabetes Testing (CDC)
metadata.heading: Types of tests

metadata.content:
- People with diabetes risk factors can ask their doctor about screening, even without symptoms.
- Doctors may test for type 1 diabetes when it is suspected or when someone is at high risk.
- Gestational diabetes is usually tested between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy, and earlier for people at higher risk.
metadata.title: Diabetes Testing (CDC)
metadata.heading: Who should talk to a doctor about testing

metadata.content: The page advises following up with a doctor, who may repeat the test to confirm the result. A single test result is not a diagnosis. Diagnosis is made by a healthcare professional. This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page.
metadata.title: Diabetes Testing (CDC)
metadata.heading: After a test at a health fair or pharmacy

metadata.content: Type 2 is the most common form of diabetes. Insulin is a hormone from the pancreas that helps move sugar from the blood into cells. In type 2 diabetes the cells do not respond to insulin normally (called insulin resistance), so blood sugar slowly rises. High blood sugar over time can lead to heart disease, vision loss and kidney disease.
metadata.title: Type 2 Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: What it is

metadata.content: Symptoms often develop slowly over several years and may go unnoticed. Sometimes there are no noticeable symptoms at all.
metadata.title: Type 2 Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Symptoms

metadata.content:
- Having prediabetes
- Being overweight
- Being 45 or older
- Having a parent, brother or sister with type 2 diabetes
- Being physically active fewer than three times a week
- Having had gestational diabetes, or having had a baby weighing 9 pounds (about 4 kg) or more
- Belonging to certain racial or ethnic groups that have higher rates in the United States, which include some Asian American people
- Having non-alcoholic fatty liver disease may also be a risk factor
metadata.title: Type 2 Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Risk factors listed on the page

metadata.content: A simple blood test can show whether someone has diabetes. If blood sugar was checked at a health fair or pharmacy, the page advises following up with a doctor to confirm the result.
metadata.title: Type 2 Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Testing

metadata.content: Type 2 diabetes can be prevented or delayed with lifestyle changes such as losing weight (if overweight), eating a healthy diet and being regularly active.
metadata.title: Type 2 Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Prevention

metadata.content:
- Diabetes is managed mostly by the person themselves, supported by their healthcare team and family.
- Some people manage it with healthy eating and activity, and others also need insulin or other medicines. Healthy eating and activity still matter when taking medicine.
- The page advises asking a doctor how often to check blood sugar and what target levels are right for the individual.
- Stress can make management harder. Regular physical activity, enough sleep and relaxation exercises may help.
- Regular visits with the healthcare team, and meeting a diabetes educator, can help.
This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page.
It does not diagnose any condition or replace a healthcare professional.
metadata.title: Type 2 Diabetes (CDC)
metadata.heading: Day-to-day management

metadata.content: The CDC page describes managing blood sugar as the key to living well with diabetes, and healthy eating as the key to managing blood sugar. The goal is to eat healthy foods, in suitable amounts, at suitable times, so that blood sugar stays within the target range as much as possible.
metadata.title: Healthy Eating (CDC)
metadata.heading: The main idea

metadata.content:
The page itself is a short overview.
It points readers to separate articles on:
- meal planning, including the plate method, carbohydrate counting and portion sizes
- choosing healthier carbohydrates
- fibre
- hidden sugars in everyday foods
- desserts and eating out
metadata.title: Healthy Eating (CDC)
metadata.heading: What the page covers

metadata.content: The page advises working with a registered dietitian or a diabetes educator to build a healthy eating plan. It does not name specific foods to include or avoid, so detailed food advice should come from that kind of professional or from other trusted sources in the knowledge base. This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page. It is not an individual diet plan.
metadata.title: Healthy Eating (CDC)
metadata.heading: Who can help

metadata.content:
When blood glucose stays high for years, the page describes risks to several parts of the body:
- **Heart and blood vessels:** higher risk of heart attack and stroke.
- **Kidneys:** kidney failure.
- **Eyes:** damage to the small blood vessels in the eye can lead to permanent vision loss.
- **Feet and nerves:** nerve damage and poor blood flow, which together raise the chance of foot ulcers, infection and, in serious cases, amputation.
- **Pregnancy:** women with gestational diabetes face higher risks during pregnancy and delivery. They, and possibly their children, also have a higher chance of type 2 diabetes later in life.
metadata.title: Diabetes (WHO fact sheet): complications, prevention and treatment
metadata.heading: Possible complications over time

metadata.content: Diabetes can be found with relatively inexpensive blood glucose tests. WHO says regular check-ups and blood tests with a healthcare provider are the best way to detect it early.
metadata.title: Diabetes (WHO fact sheet): complications, prevention and treatment
metadata.heading: Early detection

metadata.content:
The page lists these steps:
- Reach and keep a healthy body weight.
- Be physically active, with at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week.
- Eat a healthy diet and avoid sugar and saturated fat.
- Avoid tobacco.
metadata.title: Diabetes (WHO fact sheet): complications, prevention and treatment
metadata.heading: Prevention (mainly type 2 diabetes)

metadata.content:
- A healthy lifestyle is described as one of the most important parts of care.
- Type 1 diabetes requires insulin.
- Some people with type 2 diabetes also need medicines, which may include insulin. The choice of medicine is made by their healthcare team.
- People with diabetes may also need care to protect the blood vessels, kidneys, eyes and feet. This can include blood pressure management, foot care, kidney screening and regular eye examinations.
This is general educational information summarised from the WHO page.
It is not a treatment plan, and medicines should only be started, changed or stopped by a qualified healthcare professional.
metadata.title: Diabetes (WHO fact sheet): complications, prevention and treatment
metadata.heading: Care and treatment overview

metadata.content: WHO recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week for adults. The page says the WHO guidelines also cover adults living with chronic conditions, but it does not give separate figures for them on this page.
metadata.title: Physical activity (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: General recommendation for adults

metadata.content:
- Lower risk of death from any cause and from cardiovascular disease
- Lower risk of high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, some cancers and falls
- Better mental health, thinking skills (cognitive health) and sleep
- Better measures of body fat
- Helps prevent and manage noncommunicable diseases, and can reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety
metadata.title: Physical activity (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: Benefits for adults described by WHO

metadata.content: Sedentary behaviour means low-energy activity while awake, such as sitting, reclining or lying down. WHO says more sedentary time is linked to higher risks of death, cardiovascular disease, cancer and type 2 diabetes, and that people of all ages should limit the time they spend sitting. This is a general population recommendation. People with diabetes or other conditions should ask their healthcare professional which activities suit them. This is general educational information summarised from the WHO page.
metadata.title: Physical activity (WHO fact sheet)
metadata.heading: Sitting for long periods

metadata.content:
The page calls physical activity a foundation of diabetes management.
It describes these benefits:
- helps manage blood sugar
- lowers the risk of heart disease and other complications
- can improve sleep and mood
- can help with losing or keeping off weight
- can improve memory
- can help manage blood pressure
- can help lower LDL ("bad") cholesterol and raise HDL ("good") cholesterol
metadata.title: Get Active (CDC)
metadata.heading: Why it matters

metadata.content:
- At least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity every week.
- One way to reach this is about 30 minutes on most days.
- A person who is just starting can begin with something as small as a 10-minute walk after dinner and build up gradually.
- Try not to go more than 2 days in a row without being active.
metadata.title: Get Active (CDC)
metadata.heading: How much activity the page suggests

metadata.content: Walking, exercises for strength and balance, taking the stairs, yard work, dancing at home, yoga, cycling, playing outside with children, and exercising with a friend.
metadata.title: Get Active (CDC)
metadata.heading: Examples of activities mentioned

metadata.content:
- Check blood sugar before and after a walk. The page says it will likely be lower afterward.
- Ask a doctor which activities are best, and which to avoid.
- Check with a doctor before starting any new or more difficult activity.
This is general educational information summarised from the CDC page.
It is not an individual exercise plan.
metadata.title: Get Active (CDC)
metadata.heading: Safety points on the page
